subject: Year-1 capex: the budget no one prepares you for
preheader: The 3-tier reserve framework · 1925 rowhouses vs 2018 tract homes · the 6 most common first-year surprises

marketSnapshot.headline: Year-1 capex — the surprise that hits 70% of new investors
marketSnapshot.body: The biggest underwriting mistake new landlords make: using 'national average' capex assumptions (8-10% of rent annually) without adjusting for building age. A 1925 rowhouse and a 2018 tract home need different reserve budgets by an order of magnitude. The discipline: pick a capex tier based on the property's age + recent renovation history, and reserve accordingly. The hidden first-year capex bill is the cause of more 'this deal didn't work like I thought' regret than any other factor.

dealSpotter.address: Example: Tier 2 property · honest capex makes it real
dealSpotter.body: $175k 3/2 from 1958. Looks like a clean turnkey deal on the surface. The honest year-1 budget: water heater replacement (~$1,800), roof repairs or full replacement ($4,000-7,500 depending on condition), HVAC service + likely AC capacitor ($400-800). Don't 'hope' these don't fail. Budget them. The deal still pencils at 7.6% cap when you include this reserve — it's a different feeling than the 8.4% the seller's listing math implies.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Strong cap rate but $5-7k year-1 capex is the cost of admission
dealSpotter.body: $118k 1924 build. Pre-WW2 housing stock is durable but ALWAYS has deferred maintenance. Common year-1 surprises: cast-iron drain line failure ($2,500-6,000), original windows (storm windows ~$200/window), galvanized supply lines causing low pressure ($1,500-4,000 to replace). Strong cap rates are real but the year-1 reality check on older stock is part of the cost of admission.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Premium price · year-1 capex ~$1,200 · pencils cleanly
dealSpotter.body: $245k 3/2, full renovation 1-2 years ago (new HVAC, roof, kitchen, electrical, plumbing). When the seller has done the work in the last 1-2 years, year-1 capex drops dramatically — typically just minor punch-list ($500-1,500). The premium for a recently renovated property: typically $15-25k more than the un-renovated equivalent. Often worth it for first or second deal where capex variance can blow your operating budget.

blogFeature.title: How to underwrite a rental property in 60 seconds
blogFeature.excerpt: The five numbers — and the 30-second capex reality check — that decide whether a rental deal pencils. The honest triage every experienced investor runs before opening the full underwrite.

qa.question: What's the actual year-1 capex budget I should hold on a single-family rental I'm buying?
qa.answer: Three honest tiers based on building age and recent capex history. Tier 1 — turnkey or recently renovated (2-3 years): budget $800-2,000 for year 1. Punch-list items, minor service calls, maybe a single appliance replacement. Tier 2 — solid building 10-30 years old, no recent renovation: budget $3,500-6,000. Reasonable likelihood of one major system needing attention (HVAC service or partial replacement, water heater, roof patching). Tier 3 — older building (40+ years) or visible deferred maintenance: budget $6,500-12,000. High likelihood of multiple system issues surfacing. As percentage of purchase price: roughly 1% tier 1, 2-3% tier 2, 4-6% tier 3. The biggest underwriting mistake new landlords make is using 'national average' capex (8-10% of rent annually) without adjusting for building age. A 1925 rowhouse and a 2018 tract home need different reserve budgets by an order of magnitude.
